questions.q: According to the lesson's decision framework, what is the first question to ask when choosing a container?
options: How much memory is available
How elements need to be accessed — by index or by key
Whether the code will be compiled with optimizations
How many lines of code the container will require
questions.explain: The framework starts with access pattern: by index points toward vector/array/deque, by key points toward map/unordered_map.

questions.q: Why does std::vector often outperform a linked structure even for workloads with frequent insertions, contrary to naive Big-O intuition?
options: std::vector has no insertion cost at all
vector's contiguous memory layout gives it much better CPU cache locality, which dominates for iteration-heavy workloads
Linked structures are no longer supported by modern compilers
std::vector automatically converts to a linked list internally when needed
questions.explain: Cache locality from contiguous storage often outweighs a theoretically better complexity class, especially when the workload involves significant iteration alongside insertions.

questions.q: For an order book that needs fast lookup of orders by price level with no requirement on iteration order, which container fits best?
options: std::vector<Order>
std::list<Order>
std::unordered_map<double, std::vector<Order>>
std::set<double>
questions.explain: Fast lookup by key with no ordering requirement is exactly the use case for an unordered_map, here mapping each price level to the orders resting there.

questions.q: In `std::map<double, std::string, std::greater<double>> byPnLDescending;`, what does the std::greater<double> template argument do?
options: It makes the map store only values greater than zero
It supplies a custom comparator that reverses map's default ascending order to descending
It is invalid syntax — map only takes two template arguments
It converts the map into an unordered_map
questions.explain: std::map's third template parameter is a comparator; passing std::greater<double> flips the default ascending (std::less) ordering to descending.

questions.q: What is the main risk the lesson warns about when choosing std::list purely because a workload involves 'frequent insertion'?
options: std::list cannot actually insert elements efficiently
If the real workload is mostly iteration, std::list's scattered, non-contiguous nodes make iteration much slower than vector's, even though insertion itself is O(1)
std::list requires more lines of code to use than vector
std::list elements cannot be sorted
questions.explain: A container choice should match the dominant workload, not just one operation; a list's per-node heap allocations hurt iteration performance badly, which can outweigh its insertion advantage if iteration dominates.
